entities.name: François Fournier-Sarlovèze
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
François Louis Fournier-Sarlovèze (1773–1827) emerged from the crucible of the French Revolution to become one of the most audacious and controversial generals of the Napoleonic Wars, embodying the era's blend of meritocracy and martial ferocity. Born in Sarlat-la-Canéda, his career spanned two decades of relentless conflict across Europe, from the Rhine to the Iberian Peninsula and the fields of Waterloo. Renowned for his aggressive cavalry tactics and a legendary propensity for dueling, Fournier-Sarlovèze carved a reputation as "the worst subject in the army" according to Napoleon himself, yet his tactical brilliance and unwavering courage were undeniable assets to the French Empire.

His military service began in 1791, joining a chasseurs regiment. He rapidly distinguished himself during the campaigns in Germany, rising through the ranks to general of brigade by 1807. Fournier-Sarlovèze played a crucial role in the Peninsular War, notably at the Battle of Fuentes de Oñoro in May 1811, where his cavalry charges provided critical support, though his insubordination often clashed with superiors like Marshal Masséna. Despite repeated dismissals and reinstatements due to his volatile temperament and frequent duels—including a famous series of encounters with General Dupont—he consistently returned to action, eventually commanding a brigade of light cavalry during the Hundred Days campaign, fighting at Quatre Bras and Waterloo in 1815.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: François Fournier-Sarlovèze was a highly effective and controversial general whose contributions to key Napoleonic campaigns, particularly in the Peninsular War and at Waterloo, had a tangible impact on the course of major European conflicts. His legendary dueling and rebellious nature also shaped the cultural perception of the Napoleonic military officer.
